analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal-pay enforcement for women with bigger penalties, wage-discussion protections, and easier lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 116 cosponsors but sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and two of its subcommittees for 20 months, never receiving a hearing or a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten the Equal Pay Act, the 1963 law against paying women less than men for equal work. Employers would face a harder legal defense, compensatory and punitive damages, and easier class-action suits, and workers could not be punished for asking about or sharing wage information. It also directs the Labor Department to help employers voluntarily audit their pay scales and directs the EEOC to collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men doing equal work would gain a stronger legal tool to recover back pay and damages, and workers generally would gain protection against retaliation for discussing wages. Working families relying on a woman's paycheck would see depressed wages addressed.

how_it_helps.text: It narrows employers' defense: an employer claiming a pay gap is based on education, training, or experience must show the factor is job-related, was applied reasonably, and that no less-discriminatory alternative practice would serve the same business purpose [S3].
It removes the requirement that the compared jobs be within the same 'establishment,' making it easier to compare pay across a company's worksites [S3].
It makes it illegal for an employer to fire or retaliate against a worker for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, or for participating in an equal-pay case [S3].
It lets equal-pay victims collect compensatory and punitive damages, keep class actions open, and recover expert fees, and lets the Secretary of Labor seek those damages in court [S3].

It directs the Labor Department to publish voluntary guidelines so employers can evaluate their own job categories for unfair pay gaps, with a recognition program and a National Award for Pay Equity for compliant employers [S3].

It requires the EEOC to write rules collecting pay data from employers broken down by employees' sex, race, and national origin to support enforcement, while weighing the reporting burden on employers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay women less than men for comparable work would bear the cost in back pay, damages, litigation, and settlements. All covered employers would take on some new pay-data reporting and compliance work, and some of that cost could be passed to customers or workers.

drawbacks.text: Punitive damages, open-ended class actions, and expert fees would raise litigation exposure for employers well beyond current back-pay remedies, which critics say encourages lawsuits against employers even without discriminatory intent [S3].

The tightened 'bona fide factor' defense would put the burden on employers to prove their pay differences are job-related and reasonable, creating uncertainty for pay systems based on market history or negotiation [S3].
New EEOC pay-data collection by sex, race, and national origin would add recordkeeping and reporting costs for employers, a burden the bill itself directs the agency to weigh [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers experiencing pay discrimination, the bill offers a genuinely stronger remedy: easier comparisons across worksites, protection for discussing wages, and real damages rather than back pay alone. The honest cost is broader litigation exposure and reporting burdens for employers, including some who pay fairly, and the burden-of-proof shift could generate settlement pressure in close cases. The voluntary audit and award programs offset the enforcement side somewhat by rewarding employers who fix gaps on their own.

outcome.mechanism: The House speaker's allies on the Education and the Workforce Committee referred the bill to two subcommittees the month after it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act on April 9, 2003, amending the Equal Pay Act's remedies and enforcement [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 2, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
116 members cosponsored the bill: 115 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with pay gaps kept the existing, weaker enforcement regime and avoided new damages liability and reporting requirements, and the Republican-controlled committee avoided a vote that its members would have had to record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and the committee that buried it

for.role: U.S. Representative (I-VT), the bill's only non-Democratic cosponsor

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over labor law, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on the day of introduction, sent the bill to two subcommittees, and never scheduled a hearing or markup

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 116 cosponsors was a Democrat except one Independent, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action on it.

industries.note: These employers would face compensatory and punitive damages, easier class actions, and a much harder legal defense under the bill. Their interest in stopping it ran against workers seeking equal pay [S3].
Even employers without pay gaps would bear new EEOC pay-data reporting and compliance costs, though the bill pairs enforcement with voluntary self-audit guidelines and a recognition award [S3].
